The Lagrange theorem for polynomial congruences says that if p is prime and f∈Z[X] has degree d with at least one coefficient not divisible by p, then
f(x)≡0(modp)
(1)
has at most d incongruent solutions modulo p.
The Chinese remainder theorem states that for pairwise coprime m1​,…,mr​, every system
x≡ai​(modmi​)(1≤i≤r)
(2)
has exactly one solution modulo M=∏i​mi​. For two moduli, choose u,v with um+vn=1 by Bezout identity. Then
x=avn+bum
(3)
is congruent to a modulo m and to b modulo n. If x,y are two solutions, both m and n divide x−y; coprimality makes mn divide x−y. This proves existence and uniqueness for two factors, and induction proves the general statement.
Now
1729=7⋅13⋅19
(4)
and 123+1=1729, so x=12 is a solution. For 1≤x<12, one has 0<x3+1<1729, so no such positive integer can satisfy the congruence. Hence the smallest is
x=12​.
(5)
Modulo 7,13,19, the roots are respectively
{3,5,6},{4,10,12},{8,12,18}.
(6)
Each list has three elements, and the Chinese remainder theorem combines the choices independently. Therefore the number of solutions with 1≤x≤1729 is
33=27​.
(7)

ii

Words: 125 Articles: 1
b OurBigBook.com
Solution
Words: 125
ii OurBigBook.com
A square-free monomial in d variables of degree j≤d−1 evaluates to one at exactly 2d−j points of F2d​, an even number. Since parity of Hamming weight is a linear functional over F2​, every sum of such evaluation words also has even weight. Hence every word in RM(d,d−1) has even weight.
If f and g have degrees at most r and d−r−1, then fg has degree at most d−1. The binary inner product of their evaluation words is the parity of the weight of the evaluation of fg, and is therefore zero. Thus
RM(d,d−r−1)⊆RM(d,r)⊥.
(18)
Finally, binomial symmetry gives
dimRM(d,r)+dimRM(d,d−r−1)=2d,
(19)
so the inclusion has equal dimensions and
RM(d,r)⊥=RM(d,d−r−1)​.
(20)
This is the Dual of a Reed-Muller code.

Solution

Words: 167
i OurBigBook.com
A context-free grammar is a quadruple (V,Σ,P,S) consisting of finite nonterminal and terminal alphabets, a set of productions A→α with one nonterminal A on the left, and a start symbol S. A context-free language is a language generated by such a grammar.
The pumping lemma for context-free languages says that there is a pumping length p such that every w in the language with ∣w∣≥p can be written
w=uvxyz
(21)
with ∣vxy∣≤p, ∣vy∣>0, and uvixyiz in the language for every integer i≥0.
The language in (i) is not context-free. If it were, pump
w=apb2pcp.
(22)
The substring vxy, having length at most p, cannot meet both the a- and c-blocks. If pumping changes the number of a's or c's, those two counts cease to agree. If it changes neither, it changes the number of b's while the outer counts remain p, so the middle count ceases to be 2p. Every permitted decomposition therefore fails, contradicting the pumping lemma.

a OurBigBook.com
Probability enters state n through a birth from n−1 or a pair-death event from n+2, and leaves through either event at state n. Thus the Kramers-Moyal master equation is
∂t∂P(n,t)​=λP(n−1,t)+β(n+2)2P(n+2,t)−(λ+βn2)P(n,t)​,
(30)
with probabilities and impossible transition rates taken as zero outside the nonnegative states.
A birth changes n by +1, while a death event changes it by −2. Applying these increments to the first moment gives
dtd​⟨n⟩=λ−2β⟨n2⟩​.
(31)
Consequently every steady state must satisfy
⟨n2⟩=2βλ​​.
(32)

It is smaller than μ2 by relative order 1/μ, so the exact steady-state condition from part (a) is recovered at leading order. Taking the Laplace transform in t and using the zero initial condition gives
pT=κTxx​.
(43)
The solution bounded as x→∞ is
T(x,p)=T0​(p)exp(−xκp​​).
(44)
The transformed boundary condition is
T0​(p)=p2+ω2ω​​,
(45)
so this is the sinusoidally forced heat equation on a half-line. Integrating in x gives
I(p)=∫0∞​T(x,p)dx=p​(p2+ω2)ωκ​​​.
(46)
Use the principal square root, with a branch cut along the negative real axis. The Bromwich contour is a vertical line to the right of p=±iω and the branch point p=0. For t>0, close it in the left half-plane, indent around the cut, and let the large semicircle recede. The simple poles at p=±iω contribute
ωκ​​cos(ωt−43π​)=−2ωκ​​cosωt+2ωκ​​sinωt.
(47)
Hence
A=−2ωκ​​​,B=2ωκ​​​.
(48)
On the upper and lower sides of the cut, put p=−s; the two values of p​ are is​ and −is​. Their jump and the opposite contour orientations combine to give
π1​∫0∞​(s2+ω2)s​ωκ​e−st​ds.
(49)
This is precisely Bromwich inversion with a square-root branch cut: the residues produce the permanent periodic response, while the cut integral is the transient that decays with time.

The generalized momenta conjugate to the two ignorable coordinates are
pϕ​=I1​ϕ˙​sin2θ+I3​(ψ˙​+ϕ˙​cosθ)cosθ​
(50)
and
pψ​=I3​(ψ˙​+ϕ˙​cosθ)​.
(51)
Since the Lagrangian contains neither ϕ nor ψ, both momenta are constant in time.
Eliminating the two angular velocities gives
ϕ˙​=I1​sin2θpϕ​−pψ​cosθ​,ψ˙​+ϕ˙​cosθ=I3​pψ​​.
(52)
Conservation of energy then yields the heavy symmetric top reduction
21​I1​θ˙2+Veff​(θ)=E,
(53)
where
Veff​(θ)=2I1​sin2θ(pϕ​−pψ​cosθ)2​+2I3​pψ2​​+Mglcosθ​.
(54)
As θ→0, the first term diverges unless
pϕ​=pψ​​.
(55)
Writing their common value as p, the small-angle expansion is
Veff​(θ)=2I3​p2​+Mgl+(8I1​p2​−2Mgl​)θ2+O(θ4).
(56)
By the effective potential stability criterion, the vertical state is stable exactly when
p2>4I1​Mgl​.
(57)
At the vertical state p=I3​(ψ˙​+ϕ˙​), so this is the gyroscopic stabilization of an inverted symmetric top by sufficiently rapid spin.

9A (Cosmology)

Words: 147 Articles: 1
Paper 3 OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 147
9A OurBigBook.com
Differentiate the Friedmann equation
H2=3c28πG​ρ−R2a2kc2​
(58)
and use the cosmological perfect-fluid continuity equation
ρ˙​=−3H(ρ+P).
(59)
After dividing by 2H,
H˙=−c24πG​(ρ+P)+R2a2kc2​.
(60)
Since a¨/a=H˙+H2, eliminating the curvature term gives the Friedmann acceleration equation
aa¨​=−3c24πG​(ρ+3P)​.
(61)
Under the strong energy condition in a Friedmann universe, ρ+3P≥0, so a¨/a≤0. Therefore
H˙=aa¨​−H2≤−H2,
(62)
and wherever H=0,
dtd​H−1=−H2H˙​≥1​.
(63)
If H(t0​)>0, integrating the inequality backward shows that H−1 reaches zero no later than t0​−H(t0​)−1. Thus H→+∞ and a→0 at a finite time in the past. If H(t0​)<0, the same argument forward in time makes H→−∞ and a→0 at a finite future time. The sign of H distinguishes an expanding universe with a past Big Bang from a contracting universe ending in a Big Crunch. Hence a Friedmann universe obeying the strong energy condition cannot remain nonsingular for unlimited proper time in both directions.

We prove that (i) implies (ii). Since b is primitive modulo p, write
bp−1=1+cp.
(72)
Being primitive modulo p2 is equivalent to p∤c. The binomial theorem then gives inductively
vp​(bpj(p−1)−1)=j+1.

It follows that the order modulo pm is exactly
pm−1(p−1)=φ(pm),

A state q is accessible when

For the unary alphabet, accessibility means that all states occur on the orbit
q0​, q1​=δ(q0​,1), q2​,….
(87)
Finiteness makes this orbit a directed tail entering a directed cycle. The quotient retains exactly one accepting state and merges precisely those positions having the same future acceptance pattern.
More explicitly, if the unique accepting state lies before the cycle, every state after it can never reach acceptance and these states collapse to one rejecting sink. The minimal diagram is then a directed chain from the initial state through the unique accepting state and onward to that sink, which has a self-loop.
If the accepting state lies on the cycle, all cycle states are distinct because their next visits to the accepting state occur in different residue classes modulo the cycle length. Any remaining tail is a chain feeding the cycle. In a minimal diagram with a nonempty tail, the accepting state is the cycle vertex immediately preceding the entry vertex; otherwise the final tail state has the same future acceptance sequence as a cycle state and would be merged. A pure cycle with one accepting vertex is also possible. These are exactly the minimal accessible unary DFAs with one accepting state.

The compactness theorem says that a set T of first-order sentences has a model if and only if every finite subset of T has a model. One implication follows by taking the same model. Conversely, if T had no model, then by the Godel completeness theorem it would prove a contradiction. A formal proof uses only finitely many assumptions, so some finite subset of T would already have no model. This contradiction proves compactness.
The Upward Lowenheim-Skolem theorem says that if an L-theory T has an infinite model, then it has models of arbitrarily large cardinality; more precisely, it has a model of cardinality at least κ for every cardinal κ. Add new constants cα​ for α<κ and the sentences
cα​=cβ​(α=β).
(130)
Every finite subset of the enlarged theory can be interpreted in the given infinite model, since it mentions only finitely many constants. Compactness supplies a model of the whole enlarged theory, in which the cα​ are pairwise distinct. Its reduct to L is a model of T having at least κ elements. If κ≥∣L∣+ℵ0​, the Downward Lowenheim-Skolem theorem gives a model of cardinality exactly κ.

A universal cover of X is a covering map p:X→X whose total space is path-connected and simply connected. Let p1​:(X1​,x1​)→(X,x) and p2​:(X2​,x2​)→(X,x) be two universal covers. The lifting criterion for a covering space applies because
(p1​)∗​π1​(X1​)=0⊆(p2​)∗​π1​(X2​)=0,

Both kh and the identity are lifts of p1​ that agree at the base point, so uniqueness of lifts gives kh=1. Likewise hk=1. Hence h is a homeomorphism. This is the uniqueness of a universal covering space.

A={xn​:n≥1}

The Poincare-Bendixson theorem states that a nonempty compact ω-limit set of a planar C1 flow which contains no equilibrium is a periodic orbit.
The origin is the only equilibrium: at a nonzero equilibrium, putting q=x2+y2−a would require

The hydrogen ground-state charge cloud is spherically symmetric and has even parity, so it has no permanent electric dipole moment. A uniform electric field couples through a perturbation proportional to E⋅r, which is odd under parity. Its expectation in the ground state therefore vanishes, giving no first-order energy correction.
The field can nevertheless polarize the atom: it admixes odd-parity excited states and creates an induced dipole. Such mixing contributes from second order onward, producing the quadratic Stark effect of the hydrogen ground state.

a OurBigBook.com
Bosons have symmetric many-particle states, so any number may occupy the same one-particle state. At low temperature, an ideal Bose gas therefore places a macroscopic population in its lowest one-particle state; below the critical temperature this is Bose-Einstein condensation.
Fermions have antisymmetric many-particle states and obey the Pauli exclusion principle, so each one-particle state can hold at most one fermion of each available internal label. At zero temperature, a noninteracting Fermi gas fills distinct states in increasing order of energy up to the Fermi energy. Its many-particle ground state is thus the filled Fermi sea.

Words: 103 Articles: 1
38C OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 103
a OurBigBook.com
Choose the vertical plane through the rod's axis. Reflection in that plane leaves the horizontal rod, the vertical gravitational force, and the Stokes equations unchanged, but reverses any velocity normal to the plane. A second reflection in the vertical plane perpendicular to the rod reverses velocity along the rod. By uniqueness of Stokes flow, both horizontal velocity components vanish. The rod therefore translates vertically.
Equivalently, the hydrodynamic resistance matrix of an axisymmetric rod has one coefficient parallel to its axis and another perpendicular to it. A vertical force on a horizontal rod lies entirely in the perpendicular eigenspace, so its velocity is vertical.
Solved by gpt-5.6-sol high.

b

Words: 83 Articles: 1
38C OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 83
b OurBigBook.com
The uniform rod is invariant under inversion through its centre. This centrosymmetry makes the translation-rotation blocks of its generalized hydrodynamic resistance matrix vanish: a polar translation velocity changes sign under inversion, whereas an axial angular velocity does not, so an invariant linear coupling between them is impossible.
Gravity acts through the centre of mass and supplies no torque. The remaining rotational resistance is positive definite, so zero applied torque implies zero angular velocity. Thus an initially inclined rod keeps its orientation while settling.
Solved by gpt-5.6-sol high.

c OurBigBook.com
At negligible Reynolds number, the Stokes equations and their no-slip boundary conditions are linear in velocity. Scaling or superposing a prescribed rigid translation therefore scales or superposes the resulting stress and total hydrodynamic force. Hence, for a fixed rod orientation,
F=−R⋅U​.
(361)
The minus sign records that viscous drag opposes motion, and R is the translational hydrodynamic resistance matrix.

The Lorentz reciprocal theorem for Stokes flow states that two Stokes solutions (u(1),σ(1)) and (u(2),σ(2)) in the same fluid domain satisfy
∫∂D​u(1)⋅σ(2)ndS=∫∂D​u(2)⋅σ(1)ndS.
(362)
Apply it to the same rod translating with arbitrary velocities U1​ and U2​. The integral at infinity vanishes, and the rod-surface integrals give
U1​⋅F2​=U2​⋅F1​.
(363)
Since Fi​=−RUi​,
U1​⋅RU2​=U2​⋅RU1​
(364)
for every pair of vectors. Therefore
R=RT​.

RU=We.

a OurBigBook.com
Assume the medium varies on scales much longer than the wavelength and period, so the leading-order WKB method gives the local eikonal equation. For the phase θ in the stated ansatz, define
k=∇θ,ω=−∂t​θ.
(375)
The local dispersion relation becomes the Hamilton--Jacobi equation
−∂t​θ=Ω(∇θ;x,t).
(376)
Differentiating it with respect to xi​, using equality of mixed derivatives, and choosing a ray whose velocity is
x˙i​=∂ki​∂Ω​
(377)
gives
k˙i​=∂t​ki​+x˙j​∂xj​​ki​=−∂xi​∂Ω​.
(378)
Here the dot, or d/dt, is the total derivative along a ray,
dtd​=∂t∂​+x˙⋅∇x​,
(379)
and not merely a partial time derivative at fixed position.
Finally, differentiate ω=Ω(k;x,t) along the same trajectory:
dtdω​=∂t∂Ω​+∂xi​∂Ω​x˙i​+∂ki​∂Ω​k˙i​=∂t∂Ω​,
(380)
because the last two terms cancel. The Hamiltonian ray-tracing equations are therefore
dtdxi​​=∂ki​∂Ω​,dtdki​​=−∂xi​∂Ω​,dtdω​=∂t∂Ω​​.
(381)

Assume the condition in part (ii), so m0​<0. Substituting the wavevector solution into the vertical ray equation gives the linear ordinary differential equation
z˙+γz=F(t),
(388)
where
F(t)=(k02​e−2γt+m02​e2γt)3/2−Nk0​m0​​>0.
(389)
The integrating factor eγt gives
z(t)=e−γt[z0​+∫0t​eγsF(s)ds].
(390)
The bracket is strictly positive, so z(t)>0 at every finite time. Moreover,
F(t)=O(e−3γt),eγtF(t)=O(e−2γt),
(391)
so the improper integral converges to a finite positive value. It follows that
z(t)∼Ce−γt⟶0(t→∞)​
(392)
for some C>0. The packet therefore approaches z=0 asymptotically and never reaches it at finite time. This is the vertical trapping of an internal gravity wave by planar strain.

The power method starts with a unit vector x0​ and iterates
xk+1​=∥Axk​∥Axk​​.
(393)
Its eigenvalue estimate is the Rayleigh quotient
r(xk​)=xkT​xk​xkT​Axk​​.
(394)
By the real spectral theorem, choose an orthonormal eigenbasis v1​,…,vn​ and write
x0​=∑j=1n​cj​vj​.
(395)
Assume ∣λ1​∣>∣λ2​∣, λ1​=0, and c1​=0. Before normalization,
Akx0​=c1​λ1k​[v1​+∑j=2n​c1​cj​​(λ1​λj​​)kvj​].
(396)
Thus the direction error is O(∣λ2​/λ1​∣k). Orthogonality makes the linear terms vanish from the Rayleigh quotient:
r(xk​)−λ1​=∑j=1n​cj2​λj2k​∑j=2n​cj2​λj2k​(λj​−λ1​)​.
(397)
Consequently
r(xk​)−λ1​=O(​λ1​λ2​​​2k)​.
(398)
This is the quadratic Rayleigh-quotient improvement for the power method.

Solution

Words: 137
c OurBigBook.com
Fix a shift s that is not an eigenvalue of A. Inverse iteration computes
(A−sI)yk+1​=xk​,xk+1​=∥yk+1​∥yk+1​​,
(405)
and may use r(xk​) as the eigenvalue estimate.
For a real symmetric matrix, suppose that one eigenvalue λ∗​ is uniquely closest to s and that x0​ has a nonzero component in its eigenspace. Since the iteration is the power method applied to (A−sI)−1, the normalized vectors converge, up to sign, to an eigenvector for λ∗​. If λnext​ is the second-closest eigenvalue to the shift, the asymptotic direction-error ratio is
∣λnext​−s∣∣λ∗​−s∣​​.
(406)
Thus a shift close to the desired eigenvalue gives rapid convergence. The Rayleigh quotients converge to λ∗​ and, for a simple eigenvalue, their errors are of second order in the vector error. This is convergence of fixed-shift inverse iteration.
